content: Chinese herbal medicine is commonly used in China to treat diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Numerous controlled trials have been conducted to evaluate its effectiveness. This review is an update of a Cochrane review originally published in 2011. The objective of this review was to assess both the potential benefits and harms of Chinese herbal medicine for individuals with diabetic peripheral neuropathy. A comprehensive search was conducted on May 14, 2012, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and AMED. Additionally, in October 2012, searches were performed in Chinese databases such as the Chinese Biomedical Database (CBM), Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure Database (CNKI), and VIP Chinese Science and Technique Journals Database. Unpublished literature was also sought in the Chinese Conference Papers Database and the Chinese Dissertation Database. No restrictions were placed on language or publication type. The review included randomized controlled trials that investigated Chinese herbal medicine for diabetic peripheral neuropathy, with a minimum treatment duration of four weeks. Comparisons were made against placebo, no intervention, or conventional treatments. Trials that combined herbal medicine with conventional drugs and compared them to the drug alone were also included. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two authors. Additional information was sought from the authors of the included studies. A total of 49 randomized trials involving 3,639 participants were included in the review. All trials were conducted and published in China. These studies tested 38 different herbal medicines, including four single herbs, eight traditional Chinese patent medicines, and 26 self-prepared Chinese herbal compound prescriptions. The trials reported outcomes such as global symptom improvement (e.g., reduction in numbness or pain) and changes in nerve conduction velocity. However, the positive results reported in these studies were derived from trials of low methodological quality, raising concerns about their reliability. Reporting on adverse events was inadequate. Eighteen trials reported no adverse events, while two trials documented adverse events. In one of these trials, adverse events occurred in the control group, while in the other, it was unclear which group experienced the adverse events. The remaining 29 trials did not specify whether adverse events were monitored. Due to the insufficient reporting of adverse events, no conclusions can be drawn regarding the safety of Chinese herbal medicines for diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Furthermore, the low methodological quality of most trials limits the reliability of any positive findings regarding the efficacy of these treatments. Therefore, any interpretation of the results should be approached with caution. In conclusion, this systematic review found no evidence to support the objective effectiveness or safety of Chinese herbal medicines for diabetic peripheral neuropathy. To date, no well-designed, randomized, placebo-controlled trials with objective outcome measures have been conducted to evaluate these treatments.
